Okay, since I'm crafting a story, I want to include scenes like protests, a social media storm, committee hearings, and relevant legal aspects such as Article 13 of the Lisbon Treaty and the EU Withdrawal Bill in relation to animal sentience. I need to make sure to avoid any exact quotes from the input to keep it original, so I'll paraphrase instead.

```
{
  "title": "After the Sentience Vote: How a Technical Defeat Sparked a Moral Uproar",
  "subtitle": "Inside the clash of law, language and conscience over animal welfare in post‑Brexit Britain",
  "author": "Staff Reporter",
  "published_at": "2026-05-21T00:00:00Z",
  "location": "London",
  "summary": "A narrowly defeated amendment intended to transplant EU-era recognition of animal sentience into UK law ignited a fierce public reaction, revealing a rift between legal process and public perception—and testing ministers’ credibility on animal welfare.",
  "tags": ["UK politics", "Brexit", "animal welfare", "legislation", "public policy"],
  "content": [
    "Outside the Palace of Westminster, handmade placards leaned against the railings like a second set of ironwork: paw prints, hooves, wings, and slogans in thick marker pen. The drizzle smudged ink into teardrops. The protesters were not especially numerous, but they were loud, and their chants rose and fell with the buses on Parliament Street. It was the kind of British protest that looks small from the pavement and sounds much larger on the evening news.",
    "The spark was an amendment defeated by a thin margin—an attempt to lift, with careful legal tweezers, a line from European law and set it down whole in the post-Brexit statute book. The line, to many, carried more than ink: it was a promise that policy would account for the inner lives of animals. To others, it was an awkward transplant the UK could better rearticulate in its own terms.",
    "In Westminster, members insisted nothing fundamental had shifted. Ministers repeated that no one in government doubted animals feel pain or experience fear and that the vote turned on how, not whether, to enshrine those considerations. What they saw as a debate over legislative architecture, the public heard as a judgment on empathy.",
    "That disconnect metastasized online. Petitions multiplied. A rotating cast of celebrities, veterinarians, farmers and legal commentators threw their weight behind threads and explainers. Some criticized the government for backsliding; others warned against importing a clause they said was poorly drafted. The argument, like many in the Brexit era, became a referendum on trust.",
    "In committee rooms and corridors, the details were drier. The EU language—born of a different constitutional order—sits uneasily in a system that treats ministerial discretion, impact assessments and delegated powers as usual tools of the trade. The government line was simple enough: protect outcomes through domestic legislation tailored to UK institutions, not by stapling foreign phrasing into a bill designed to tidy the statute book.",
    "Yet animal welfare has always been more than a technical field note. It is a cultural barometer, cutting across party lines and drawing together people who rarely share causes. Farmers wary of onerous regulation nonetheless speak of stewardship. Urban pet owners, distant from abattoirs and fields, still vote with a moral imagination populated by foxes, beagles and battery hens. To them, the amendment looked less like an obscure fix and more like a signal flare.",
    "In the days after the vote, MPs’ inboxes filled. A veterinary association warned that loosening a clear, overarching recognition would fray standards over time. Campaigners reminded Parliament that, across Europe, sentience provisions had become a platform for phasing out some practices but had failed to reach others—proof, they argued, that a sentence is not a panacea but is still a compass.",
    "Backbenchers hostile to importing the clause countered that the UK has often outpaced its neighbors on welfare: stronger bans, tighter inspections, tougher penalties. Why, they asked, would the country that went further need Brussels’ words to go further again? Better, they said, to write a domestic law that binds ministers to consult science and ethics, and to publish transparent justifications, than to rely on a general statement open to contest in the courts.",
    "The politics are febrile. After years of procedural trench warfare, the public’s appetite for explanation is thin. To insist it is all about process, not principle, is to overlook how often process has been wielded like principle. And for a government eager to project both competence and compassion, the optics of voting down the clearest statement of sentience proved difficult to wash away.",
    "Privately, officials sketch a path out: a bespoke bill recognizing animal sentience in UK law, a statutory committee to scrutinize how policies affect welfare, and a duty on ministers to respond publicly to its findings. It would be a homegrown framework with measurable teeth—less a borrowed slogan than an operating manual.",
    "Whether that will satisfy those huddled in the rain is less certain. They do not want a syllogism; they want a safeguard that looks like one. They want the country, at a time when much feels transactional, to say plainly what it stands for. In politics, words do not just bind governments. They bind time.",
    "As the crowd thinned and the banners dripped toward the pavement, a spaniel in a yellow raincoat tugged its owner toward the curb. The dog did not know about statutes or treaties. It knew only that the air smelled of wet wool and diesel, and that something important was happening behind the gates. In that small, ordinary tug lay the paradox Parliament is trying to write into law: a being that cannot speak for itself, demanding, all the same, to be heard."
  ]
}
```
